turns.q:
Your response was: "It's quite clear and easy to follow at first glance, though I'd need more time to be sure about how it handles specific edge cases. The layout for the payment details seems straightforward, but from a governance perspective, that would need a proper clinical review regarding data security protocols. I also noticed the order summary section, which is very prominent, although I'd need to look at the full workflow before I could comment on its overall effectiveness."

We want to understand what you meant by "I also noticed the order summary section, which is very prominent", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The Order Summary card is positioned at the top of the checkout layout, above the Payment Details section, making it the first major content area in the hierarchy.  
B) The Total line in the Order Summary is visually emphasized with larger, bolder text than the item details, making the final amount especially noticeable.  
C) The Order Summary occupies a large boxed section with item names, quantities, subtotal, shipping, and total grouped together, making the purchase information feel strongly foregrounded.  
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: I’d choose C. What I was responding to was the whole order summary being presented as a large boxed section, with the item names, quantities, subtotal, shipping, and total all grouped together before the user gets to payment. It gives the purchase information quite a lot of visual weight, almost as if that is the main task on the screen. The payment area is clear, but it sits underneath something that feels very dominant initially.

turns.q: What information were you trying to verify when the large Order Summary box stood out to you, and what would you change about that grouping?
turns.a: I was trying to verify whether the amounts reconciled cleanly, because the $39.99 is very visually prominent beside the Wireless Mouse, while the final payable amount is $288.99 lower down. In a clinical setting I’m very used to checking that the displayed headline figure matches the actual action being taken, and here my eye has to do a little extra work to connect item prices, subtotal, shipping, and total. I’d keep the grouping, because it is useful, but I’d make the final total the clearest figure in the card and reduce the visual dominance of the individual item price. I’d also consider labelling the summary more explicitly as a read-only review, so it doesn’t feel like a separate step before payment.

turns.q: What would need to be clearer or less prominent in the Order Summary layout for you to feel the subtotal, shipping, and total reconcile correctly at a glance?
turns.a: The main thing I’d want clearer is the relationship between the two item prices on the right and the subtotal line beneath them. At the moment, the Wireless Mouse price is much larger and bolder than the chair price, so it interrupts the arithmetic visually even though it’s just one line item. I’d make both item prices the same weight and size, then give the final $288.99 next to Total the strongest emphasis, not just the word “Total” itself. That would let the eye move in a more reliable sequence: item prices, subtotal, shipping, final amount.

turns.q: You mentioned wanting the final $288.99 next to Total to have the strongest emphasis; what about the current Order Summary hierarchy makes that hard to achieve?
turns.a: What makes it difficult is that the hierarchy is split in an odd way: the word “Total” is very strong on the left, but the actual $288.99 on the right is comparatively quiet. Meanwhile, the $39.99 for the Wireless Mouse is the boldest numeric value in the card, so clinically speaking, my eye treats that as the figure requiring attention even though it is not the amount the user is about to authorise. I’d expect the payable amount to be the single clearest number, because that is the decision point before entering card details. At the moment, the emphasis is attached to the wrong number, and the final amount has to be inferred rather than immediately confirmed.

turns.q: Looking at the Order Summary box as a visual grouping, which part first pulled your eye before you noticed the $39.99 and final Total emphasis issue?
turns.a: Before the numbers, it was the sheer size and placement of the Order Summary card itself that pulled my eye. It sits right at the top under “Secure Checkout,” with a large amount of white space and a full border around it, so it reads as the first governed area of the task, if I can put it that way. The pale “ORDER SUMMARY” label is actually quite subtle, so my attention goes more to the item rows and the overall block than to the heading. I think that framing makes me start reviewing the contents before I even orient myself to the payment action below.
